mcqs.question: An interviewer confirms the input array is already sorted. Which change to your plan does that most directly justify?
options: Dropping a hash-set approach in favor of two pointers or binary search
Switching from recursion to iteration for stack safety
Assuming there are no duplicate values
Skipping the empty-input edge case entirely
mcqs.explanation: Sortedness is what makes two pointers and binary search viable in the first place, so it's the constraint that most directly reshapes which algorithm family applies. Sortedness says nothing about duplicates or emptiness — those are separate questions that still need asking.

mcqs.question: The prompt states n can be up to 10^9. What does that constraint rule out?
options: Any solution that uses recursion
Any approach with an O(n) or worse pass over the input
Any solution that uses a hash map
Any approach that returns a negative number
mcqs.explanation: At n ~ 10^9, even a single linear pass is too slow, so the constraint is pointing at O(log n) or O(1) approaches like binary search on the answer or a closed-form calculation. Recursion and hash maps aren't disqualified by size alone — only their complexity class matters, and a hash map lookup is O(1) per call regardless.

mcqs.question: What actually distinguishes a clarifying question worth asking from one that isn't?
options: Whether it's about the input's constraints rather than the environment
Whether the interviewer already expects to hear it
Whether your approach would genuinely differ depending on the answer
Whether it can be answered with a simple yes or no
mcqs.explanation: The real test is whether both possible answers lead you down a different path — if your plan is identical either way, the question added nothing regardless of its topic or phrasing. Plenty of constraint-sounding questions still fail this test, and plenty of yes/no questions pass it.

mcqs.question: A candidate asks "should I optimize for time or space?" before having any second approach in mind. What's the problem with that question?
options: It's phrased as a closed question instead of an open one
There's no actual trade-off on the table yet, so the question has nothing concrete to attach to
Interviewers never answer trade-off questions honestly
It should have been asked after coding instead of before
mcqs.explanation: A time/space trade-off question only means something once you have two candidate solutions that actually trade one for the other — asked before that, it's outsourcing your own design thinking rather than confirming a real fork. Timing and phrasing aren't the actual issue; the missing substance is.

mcqs.question: You silently assume the input has no duplicates, code accordingly, and the assumption turns out to be correct. Why does this still read worse than stating the assumption out loud?
options: It doesn't — a correct assumption is exactly as good as a confirmed one
Because the interviewer needed to hear you say the word "duplicates"
Because silent assumptions always produce buggy code even when they happen to hold
The interviewer has no way to tell you reasoned about the risk rather than got lucky
mcqs.explanation: The value of stating an assumption isn't correctness in that one instance — it's making the reasoning visible, so a lucky guess and a deliberate, defensible choice don't look identical from the interviewer's side. Silent assumptions aren't inherently buggy; they're just unverifiable as reasoning.
